910.name: Dacian Heritage & Roman Dacia
910.description: The territory of modern Moldova was part of the Dacian cultural sphere. Roman influence from the conquest of neighbouring Dacia (106 CE) brought partial romanisation, while successive migrations of Goths, Huns, and Slavic peoples reshaped the population.

sub_clusters.name: Dacian & Geto-Dacian Culture
sub_clusters.description: The Getae and Dacians inhabited the region between the Carpathians and the Dniester. Burebista's Dacian kingdom (82–44 BCE) briefly unified Dacian tribes. Trajan's conquest of Dacia (106 CE) brought Roman colonists and partial romanisation.

sub_clusters.name: Migration Period
sub_clusters.description: Following Roman withdrawal from Dacia (271 CE), successive waves of Goths, Huns, Gepids, Avars, and Slavs passed through or settled in Moldovan territory, contributing to the region's ethnic transformation.

920.name: Medieval Moldavia & Statehood
920.description: After centuries under Slavic, Cuman, and Mongol influence, the Principality of Moldavia was founded (1359) under Bogdan I. Stephen the Great (r. 1457–1504) became Moldova's greatest ruler, defending the principality against Ottoman, Hungarian, and Polish threats.

sub_clusters.name: Early Medieval Period & Founding of Moldavia
sub_clusters.description: Slavic settlement, Pecheneg and Cuman nomadic control, Mongol/Golden Horde suzerainty, and the founding of the Principality of Moldavia by Bogdan I (1359) after breaking away from Hungarian vassalage.

sub_clusters.name: Stephen the Great & Moldavian Golden Age
sub_clusters.description: Stephen the Great (Ștefan cel Mare, r. 1457–1504) defended Moldavia in 36 battles, notably defeating the Ottomans at Vaslui (1475). He built 40 churches and monasteries, earning recognition from Pope Sixtus IV as 'Athlete of Christ'.
key_events: Stephen the Great's victory at Battle of Vaslui (January 10, 1475)

930.name: Ottoman Suzerainty & Phanariot Era
930.description: Moldavia became an Ottoman vassal state, retaining internal autonomy but paying heavy tribute. The Phanariot period (1711–1821) saw Greek-origin rulers appointed by Constantinople, increasing Ottoman control and cultural influence.

sub_clusters.name: Ottoman Vassalage
sub_clusters.description: Moldavia under Ottoman suzerainty retained its Orthodox faith, legal system, and boyar class but paid increasing tribute. Dimitrie Cantemir's failed alliance with Peter the Great of Russia (1711) ended native-born rule.

sub_clusters.name: Phanariot Period
sub_clusters.description: Greek Phanariot princes appointed by the Ottoman Sultan ruled Moldavia, introducing fiscal exploitation but also Enlightenment ideas. The Treaty of Bucharest (1812) ceded Bessarabia (eastern Moldavia) to the Russian Empire.

940.name: Russian Bessarabia & Romanian Context
940.description: Russia's annexation of Bessarabia (1812) separated it from the rest of Moldavia, which later united with Wallachia to form Romania (1859). Bessarabia experienced Russification, Jewish immigration, and economic underdevelopment under tsarist rule.

sub_clusters.name: Tsarist Annexation & Russification
sub_clusters.description: Russia's annexation of Bessarabia in 1812, the establishment of Russian administrative control, Russification of education and administration, and the settlement of diverse ethnic communities (Germans, Bulgarians, Gagauz).

sub_clusters.name: Late Imperial Era & National Awakening
sub_clusters.description: The Congress of Berlin (1878) confirmed Russian control. Bessarabia remained an agrarian backwater with widespread poverty. The 1905–1907 unrest, WWI disruption, and the Russian Revolution enabled Bessarabian national mobilisation.

950.name: Romanian Unification & Soviet Annexation
950.description: Bessarabia voted for union with Romania (1918) but was annexed by the Soviet Union (1940/1944) following the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. The Moldavian SSR was created, imposing Soviet identity on a Romanian-speaking population.

sub_clusters.name: Union with Romania
sub_clusters.description: The Sfatul Țării (Country Council) voted for union with Romania (March 27, 1918). Romanian administration brought land reform but also cultural tensions. The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact's secret protocol (1939) assigned Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere.

sub_clusters.name: Soviet Annexation & WWII
sub_clusters.description: Soviet ultimatum and annexation (June 1940), Romanian-German recapture (1941–1944), the Holocaust of Bessarabian Jews (Transnistria deportations), and the final Soviet re-annexation (August 1944), followed by mass deportations and famine.

950.name: Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic
950.description: The Moldavian SSR imposed a separate 'Moldovan' identity, Cyrillic script, and Sovietisation on the Romanian-speaking population. Collectivisation, Russification, and the creation of an industrial base in Transnistria shaped Soviet Moldova.

sub_clusters.name: Stalinism & Collectivisation
sub_clusters.description: Post-war deportations of 'bourgeois elements', forced collectivisation, the 1946–1947 famine (killing tens of thousands), Russification of education, and the imposition of Cyrillic script on the 'Moldovan language'.

sub_clusters.name: Late Soviet Period & National Revival
sub_clusters.description: Agricultural and wine-producing focus, continuation of Russification, Gorbachev-era glasnost enabling a language movement (1989 language law restoring Latin script), the Popular Front of Moldova, and the declaration of sovereignty (1990).

960.name: Independence & Transnistria Conflict
960.description: Moldova declared independence (August 27, 1991) but immediately faced the Transnistria secessionist conflict. Europe's poorest country has oscillated between pro-European and pro-Russian orientations, with EU candidate status achieved in 2022.

sub_clusters.name: Early Independence & Transnistria War
sub_clusters.description: Independence declaration (August 27, 1991), the brief Transnistria War (1992) resulting in a frozen conflict with Russian troops stationed in the breakaway region, economic collapse, and mass emigration.

sub_clusters.name: European Integration Path
sub_clusters.description: Oscillation between pro-EU and pro-Russian governments. The 2009 'Twitter Revolution', Association Agreement with the EU (2014), banking fraud scandal ($1 billion, 2014), Maia Sandu's pro-EU presidency (2020), EU candidate status (June 2022), and the impact of Russia's Ukraine invasion on Moldova's security and energy.
